description: Solo developer building EcoSphere-4D: an interactive 3D climate and Earth exploration web app using Three.js and real-time data visualization. Passionate about astronomy, web development, and environmental data science.
summary: EcoSphere-4D is an interactive 3D climate and Earth exploration web application built using Three.js and real-time data visualization. Developed as a solo project for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it addresses the "Be An Earth System Trend Detective" challenge by allowing users to seamlessly explore, select, and visualize multi-variable Earth science data. The platform translates complex environmental trends over time into an intuitive 3D spatial experience, helping researchers and enthusiasts instantly determine significant ecological shifts, regional variations, and underlying climate patterns
details:
I'm Youssef, and I built ECOSPHERE-4D on my own for this challenge. It's a 3D Earth you can spin, zoom into and ask questions. I wanted one place where you can see what the planet is doing today and where current trends may lead.

The globe mixes three kinds of data, and I labelled each one so nobody confuses them. REAL is NASA data: GIBS satellite imagery, POWER temperature records (tap any spot and you get its warming trend since 1990) and EONET storms and wildfires. LIVE is current wind, clouds, sea temperature and ocean currents from Open-Meteo, plus official storm tracks from NOAA and JTWC. FUTURE is the IPCC AR6 scenarios, from SSP1-1.9 to SSP5-8.5, always shown with their uncertainty ranges. You can drag a time machine from 2000 to 2100 and watch temperature, sea level and the share of ocean warm enough to feed cyclones change.

One thing I cared about is that storms aren't just icons. They come from real reports, and they affect the planet around them: they thicken the clouds, leave a cold trail in the sea and push the ocean currents. If a storm's last official report is more than 48 hours old, I hide it instead of pretending it's still active.

I built it so students and curious people can explore climate data without jumping between many websites. It's not meant for safety or emergency decisions, and the Sources panel says clearly what is observed, forecast or modelled.

It's one HTML file using JavaScript and Three.js, hosted on Vercel. Since all the data comes from free public APIs, I added a loading screen that checks each feed and explains what went wrong if a connection fails.
